specAnchors.text: describe the stages in the nitrogen cycle, including the roles of nitrogen fixing bacteria, decomposers, nitrifying bacteria and denitrifying bacteria (specific names of bacteria are not required)

primer.text: Nitrogen gas fills the sky, yet living things cannot absorb it directly. This note walks the nitrogen cycle: fixing bacteria converting gas into nitrates, feeding passing proteins up the food chain, decomposers returning ammonia, and denitrifying bacteria handing nitrogen back to the air.

modules.title: Fixing Nitrogen for Life
modules.opening: The air is nearly four-fifths nitrogen gas, yet plants cannot drink it straight from the sky, so nitrogen fixing bacteria first convert that gas into ammonium compounds and then into the nitrates that roots can absorb.
keyPoints: Nitrogen exists as N2 gas in the atmosphere and inside proteins in living tissues.
Nitrogen fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds, which become nitrates in the soil.
Some fixers live free in the soil, while others occupy root nodules of leguminous plants in a mutualistic partnership.
Lightning and fertiliser production can also fix nitrogen, and plants then absorb the nitrates to build proteins.

low.restatement: Bacteria unlock the gas in the air and turn it into soil food for plants.
low.analogy: A currency exchange at the border: cash nobody local accepts is converted into coins every shop will take.
low.examPointer: Name the sequence — nitrogen gas, ammonium compounds, nitrates — and mention the root nodules of leguminous plants.

medium.restatement: Fixation is the gateway of the whole cycle because atmospheric nitrogen is inert: free-living and nodule-dwelling bacteria reduce N2 into ammonium compounds, soil chemistry converts those into nitrates, and roots absorb the nitrates to assemble plant proteins.
medium.analogy: A smithy forging raw ore into nails a carpenter can actually use.
medium.examPointer: For the fixation question, always name the bacterial converters and the final absorbable ion — nitrates.

modules.title: Nitrogen Riding the Food Chain
sourceHeadings: Transfer of nitrogen between living organisms
modules.opening: Once a plant has built protein from nitrates, every bite passes that nitrogen up the food chain, from herbivore to carnivore, one digestive step at a time.
keyPoints: Animals feed on plants and digest the plant proteins, gaining nitrogen for their own animal proteins.
Nitrogen passes from one consumer to the next along the chain in the same fashion.
Every level of the chain depends on the fixed nitrogen that entered through the plants.

low.restatement: Eating passes nitrogen from plants into animals, and from animals into bigger animals.
low.analogy: A parcel handed along a line of couriers, each one adding their own wrapping.
low.examPointer: Say digestion: nitrogen arrives inside proteins and is rebuilt into the proteins of the eater.

medium.restatement: Digestion breaks plant protein into usable nitrogen, which the herbivore rebuilds into animal protein; each predator then repeats the step, so the nitrogen climbs the chain one digestion at a time, anchored by the nitrates plants absorbed.
medium.analogy: A relay where the baton is remade slightly at every handover but never leaves the track.
medium.examPointer: Link the feeding step to protein building — that pairing carries the marks.

modules.title: Recycling Nitrogen Back to the Air
modules.opening: Death and waste are not the end of nitrogen: decomposers return it to the soil as ammonia, nitrifying bacteria rebuild it into nitrates, and denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged ground finally hand it back to the air.
keyPoints: Decomposers return nitrogen from dead organisms and waste to the soil as ammonia.
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrites and onwards into nitrates, a process called nitrification.
Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, and they work hardest in anaerobic, waterlogged soil.
Farmers plough soil to add air, which reduces denitrification.

low.restatement: Rotting returns nitrogen to the soil, rebuilding makes it useful again, and denitrifying bacteria send the rest skyward.
low.analogy: A recycling depot: waste dropped off, sorted back into usable stock, and the leftovers shipped out of town.
low.examPointer: Quote the nitrification sequence — ammonia, nitrites, nitrates — and link denitrification to waterlogged soil.

medium.restatement: Decomposers strip nitrogen from corpses and waste into ammonia; nitrifying bacteria oxidise it through nitrites into nitrates for plant uptake; in oxygen-poor ground denitrifying bacteria reduce the nitrates back to nitrogen gas, which ploughing counteracts by aerating the soil.
medium.analogy: A three-stage water filter that can also dump everything back into the river when the drains clog.
medium.examPointer: Name all four bacterial roles — fixing, decomposing, nitrifying, denitrifying — since the spec groups them together.

glossary.definition: The conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds by nitrogen fixing bacteria.
The swellings on the roots of leguminous plants that house nitrogen fixing bacteria.
The ions in soil that plant roots absorb to build plant proteins.
The conversion of ammonia into nitrites and onwards into nitrates by nitrifying bacteria.
The conversion of nitrates back into nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria.

figures.alt: Diagram illustrating the nitrogen cycle, showing processes like nitrogen fixation, nitrification, denitrification, and the role of plants, animals, and bacteria.
